# The Hateful Immortals: A Domestic History in Documents

**Dr. Amelia Thornton**
*Brennan Chair of Parahuman Studies, Columbia University*

---

## Preface & Acknowledgments

This monograph would not have been possible without the cooperation of its subjects, who granted access to personal correspondence spanning nearly two centuries with a reluctance I can only describe as mutually enthusiastic obstruction. I am indebted to the National Registry of Anomalous Persons (NRAP) for declassifying the Wynn-Alderton file under the 2019 Transparency in Parahuman Affairs Act; to the Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo in Lisbon for locating two hotel receipts I was assured did not exist; and to my research assistant, Daniel Pham, who transcribed fourteen hours of interview tape and emerged, I believe, a changed man.

All documents are reproduced with permission. Footnotes are my own unless otherwise attributed. Bracketed insertions indicate editorial clarification. I have attempted, throughout, to maintain the dispassionate evidentiary standard appropriate to institutional scholarship.

I have not always succeeded.

—A.T., New York, 2024

---

## I. Foundational Documents

### 1.1 Certificate of Marriage

The record is held in the Municipal Archives of the City of Boston, filed under civil unions for the year 1847. It is unremarkable in every respect save longevity.

>**CERTIFICATE OF MARRIAGE**
>
>Commonwealth of Massachusetts
>County of Suffolk
>
>This is to certify that on the 14th day of June, in the Year of Our Lord 1847, **James Alcott Wynn**, aged twenty-four years, of Charlestown, and **Margaret Elise Alderton**, aged twenty-two years, of Beacon Hill, were united in Marriage in accordance with the laws of the Commonwealth.
>
>Officiant: Rev. Tobias Finch, Second Congregational Church
>Witnesses: Edmund R. Wynn, Clara Alderton-Hewes
>
>Filed this 16th day of June, 1847.

A photographic reproduction shows the document in excellent condition, which is to say better condition than any paper artifact from 1847 has a right to be in. Margaret, as will become relevant, kept it in an acid-free portfolio she purchased in 1972, long before acid-free portfolios were widely available to the public. She had noticed the yellowing. She noticed everything.

James, when I asked him about the certificate's preservation, said: "That's Margaret's department. I can't be killed, but I can't be bothered either."[^1]

[^1]: Interview, 14 March 2024. Margaret, seated beside him, immediately responded: "You said nearly the exact same thing in 1953, except you said 'I can't be bothered with paper.' You were sitting in the kitchen of the Recoleta apartment, wearing a brown vest I'd mended twice, and you were eating a pear." James: "You see what I live with?" Margaret: "You don't *live with* anything. That's the whole problem."

### 1.2 Attestations of Specialness

The term is archaic, belonging to a period of American parahuman governance (roughly 1831–1909) in which abilities were catalogued under the delicate euphemism "Specialness," as if the federal government were writing report cards for gifted children.[^2] Two attestations survive from the Wynn-Alderton file.

[^2]: The 1831 Parahuman Identification Act was the first federal attempt to register individuals with anomalous capacities. Its language is a masterwork of bureaucratic discomfort: abilities are referred to as "gifts of constitution," their bearers as "persons of special endowment." One imagines the congressional authors blushing as they wrote.

>**ATTESTATION OF SPECIALNESS**
>United States Department of the Interior
>Bureau of Special Census
>
>Subject: ALDERTON, Margaret Elise (Mrs. James A. Wynn)
>Date of Examination: 3 November 1847
>Location: Federal Building, Boston, MA
>
>**Nature of Specialness:** Subject demonstrates total and perfect recall of all sensory experience from approximately the age of three years, two months to the present. Subject was read a sequence of 200 randomized words and reproduced them without error in forward and reverse order. Subject was then asked to describe the clothing worn by each of the four examiners. Descriptions were accurate to the thread count.[^3] Subject reports that memories do not degrade, diminish, or lose sensory specificity with time. Subject reports no capacity to selectively forget, suppress, or attenuate any remembered experience.
>
>**Classification:** Mnemonic, Total. Grade: Singular.
>
>**Examiner's Note:** Subject wept briefly during the examination. When asked why, she stated: "I was remembering my father's hands. He died in April. Every time I look at my own hands I see his. It does not fade. It will never fade." Examiner recommends no further comment on this point.

[^3]: Thread count. One pauses to consider what living inside such a mind would be like—not for a day or a year, but for a hundred and seventy-seven years. Every harsh word preserved in original fidelity. Every kindness, too, but we are not wired to weigh kindnesses and cruelties on the same scale, and Margaret's gift—or condition, or sentence—does not permit the merciful blurring that allows the rest of us to remain married, or sane, or both.

>**ATTESTATION OF SPECIALNESS**
>United States Department of the Interior
>Bureau of Special Census
>
>Subject: WYNN, James Alcott
>Date of Examination: 3 November 1847
>Location: Federal Building, Boston, MA
>
>**Nature of Specialness:** Subject demonstrates complete biological indestructibility. Subject was struck with a regulation iron bar across the left forearm with no resulting injury, bruising, or expression of discomfort. Subject was exposed to an open flame applied to the dorsal surface of the right hand for a period of thirty seconds; no burn was observed. Subject cheerfully[^4] submitted to additional trials including but not limited to: a fall from a second-story window (landed on his feet, brushed off his trousers), ingestion of a solution of arsenic trisulfide (requested a glass of water afterward "to wash the taste out"), and a point-blank discharge of a .44 caliber pistol directed at the left thigh (the bullet flattened against the skin and fell to the floor; subject picked it up and asked to keep it as a souvenir).
>
>**Classification:** Corporeal, Invulnerable. Grade: Absolute.
>
>**Examiner's Note:** Subject appears to genuinely enjoy the testing process. His wife, observing from the gallery, did not.

[^4]: *Cheerfully*. I have by now spent enough time with James Wynn to confirm that this adverb is, if anything, understated. He treats his indestructibility with the breezy nonchalance of a man who has never, in 201 years of life, had a reason to be afraid. This is, as Margaret has observed on multiple occasions across multiple centuries, "the single most irritating thing about him, and the competition is fierce."

### 1.3 Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (First Instance)

>**PETITION FOR DISSOLUTION OF MARRIAGE**
>
>Commonwealth of Massachusetts
>Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas
>
>Filed: 12 February 1848
>
>Petitioner: Margaret E. Wynn (née Alderton)
>Respondent: James A. Wynn
>
>GROUNDS: Irreconcilable difference of temperament.
>
>**COURT DISPOSITION:** Denied. Presiding Judge H. W. Lowell notes that a marriage of eight months' duration has not yet had sufficient opportunity to develop irreconcilable differences, and counsels the petitioner to exercise patience.

Eight months. They had been married eight months.

What is known about that eight-month interval is scant. The court record tells us nothing. The Bureau of Special Census file contains no correspondence from this period. The couple's families—the prosperous, respectable Aldertons; the striving, slightly less prosperous Wynns—left no letters referencing any marital difficulty, which either means there was none visible from the outside, or that both families were engaged in the kind of disciplined silence that Victorian propriety demanded and that Margaret, with typical precision, would later describe as "the family talent for pretending the house wasn't burning while standing in the ashes."[^5]

[^5]: Letter to her sister Clara, 1861. The full letter is remarkable and will be discussed in Section II. For now, the relevant point is that Margaret's metaphors, unlike her memory, are not literal: the house was not burning. James, after all, would have survived it.

What we do have is a single letter, discovered not in the official file but in a private collection—the Alderton-Hewes papers, donated to the Massachusetts Historical Society in 1987 by a descendant who appears to have had no idea what was in the box.[^6]

[^6]: The box was labeled "Misc. Correspondence, Pre-Civil War." One can only marvel at the curatorial standards of the Alderton-Hewes estate.

### 1.4 Letter, Margaret Wynn to James Wynn, Undated [Internal Evidence Suggests August 1847]

>*My Dearest, Most Impossible James—*
>
>*You have been gone two hours. This is a fact I report with scientific detachment, as befits a woman of Special endowment: two hours, fourteen minutes, and I think roughly thirty seconds, though I confess I was not attending the clock at the exact moment of your departure because I was still laughing at what you said about Reverend Finch's sermon, which I will not commit to paper in case this letter is read by persons of moral sensitivity but which I have committed, as I commit everything, to the deep and permanent archive of all I have witnessed, where it will remain, bright and whole, when I am very old and when perhaps nothing else is funny anymore.*
>
>*I wish to lodge a complaint. Two hours is too long. My memory is a curse in this regard: I can recall the precise pressure of your hand on the small of my back as we danced on Tuesday—the exact weight of it, the warmth of each finger through the muslin—and the recall is so perfect that it produces a kind of agony, because the memory is not the thing, and I want the thing, and I want it now, and you are in Charlestown attending to your mother's chimney, which I do not regard as a sufficient reason for absence.*
>
>*Come home. I have memorized you completely. Every freckle, every eyelash, that ridiculous scar above your left eyebrow that you cannot even explain because you got it before your Specialness manifested and you were, apparently, an ordinary clumsy boy who walked into a stable door. I have the entire catalog. And yet I find that I want to check the original against the record. I want to verify. This is, I think, what people mean when they say love, but they experience it through a fog, and I experience it in terrible clarity, and I do not know if that is better or worse but I know that I would not trade it, not for anything, not for the sweet blurring that everyone else gets to hide inside.*
>
>*Hurry.*
>
>*Your Margaret*
>
>*P.S. I have eaten the last of the pears. You will survive this, as you survive everything. I, however, may not survive another two hours without you, and I have no Specialness to protect me from that particular destruction.*

I include the letter in full because it will not come again—this voice, this unguarded, incandescent certainty. Not because Margaret's capacity for love diminishes. It does not. That is, in many ways, the problem.

What follows is 177 years.

## II. The Catalogue of Centuries

### 2.1 Boston and the Early Decades (1847–1879)

The first three decades of the Wynn marriage are, archivally, the thinnest. This is not unusual for the period—private correspondence was less frequently preserved, and the couple had not yet developed the habit, later almost compulsive, of documenting their arguments in writing, which Margaret would eventually describe as "leaving evidence for the prosecution" and James would describe as "Margaret's favorite hobby after being angry."[^7]

[^7]: Audio recording, Buenos Aires, 1957. James's voice is warm and amused on the tape. Margaret's reply—"My *favorite* hobby is being right. Being angry is merely the cost of living with a man who never learns"—is not warm. It is, however, precise.

What survives from this period: twenty-three letters between Margaret and her sister Clara, six legal filings (four additional divorce petitions, all denied, and two property disputes with neighbors), a brief mention in a Boston Globe society column from 1859 describing Mrs. Wynn as "handsome, possessed of a remarkable memory for social slights, and widely feared at dinner parties," and a single letter from James to his brother Edmund that contains the earliest recorded instance of a pattern that will define the next century and a half.

>*…I said what I said about her mother and I will not unsay it, for the woman IS a pestilent harridan, though I grant I ought not to have said so at Christmas dinner and perhaps not in those exact words. But here is the thing of it, Edmund—Maggie will forgive me. She must. It has only been four years. We have forever. That is the whole gift of what we are. She may rage at me for a decade, for two decades; I will still be here when the storm passes, and she will see that I have not left, and cannot be driven off, and that in itself is a kind of proof, is it not?*[^8]

[^8]: One might observe, with the benefit of hindsight, that James Wynn here articulates a theory of marriage that contains both a profound truth and a catastrophic miscalculation. The truth: presence is a form of devotion. The miscalculation: assuming that endurance and resolution are the same thing. He could not be driven off. He could not be killed. He could not, in any physical sense, be hurt. What he could be, and what Margaret would spend the next 173 years making him, was *accountable*—to every word, in its exact original phrasing, forever.

The "harridan" remark, as it is referred to in later correspondence with a frequency that suggests canonical status, appears to have been made at Christmas dinner in 1851. Margaret's mother, Eloise Alderton, had questioned whether James was providing adequately for her daughter. The exact wording of what followed is preserved, naturally, only in Margaret's memory, but the substance is consistent across every subsequent citation: James called Eloise Alderton a pestilent harridan who had "the temperament of a hornet and the conversational grace of a blocked drain."

He said this in front of Margaret's parents, her sister, her brother-in-law, and—a detail Margaret would later append to the charge sheet with prosecutorial relish—a visiting minister.

Margaret's fifth divorce petition was filed the following January.

>**PETITION FOR DISSOLUTION OF MARRIAGE**
>
>Filed: 8 January 1852
>
>Petitioner: Margaret E. Wynn
>Respondent: James A. Wynn
>
>GROUNDS: Cruelty of language and manner; persistent failure to apologize; fundamental unsuitability of temperament.
>
>**COURT DISPOSITION:** Denied. Judge Lowell, who had denied the first four petitions and by now appears to have developed a certain weary familiarity with the Wynns, writes: "The petitioner's grievances, while vivid in their specificity, do not constitute cruelty as defined by statute. The Court notes that the respondent, far from abandoning the marital home, appears almost aggressively determined to remain in it. This is not grounds for dissolution. This is, regrettably, marriage."

By the late 1870s, the Wynns faced a problem that had nothing to do with their marriage, though it would become permanently entangled with it: they were not aging. James, at fifty-six, appeared to be a man of twenty-four. Margaret, at fifty-four, could have passed for a woman who had just turned twenty-two. Neighbors had begun to notice.
